title: Date and publication
short: Dated 21 February 1825 and first printed in 1828, as 'Lines Composed on a Day in February' in The Bijou and in Coleridge's Poetical Works.
body: The poem's subtitle in collected editions, 'Lines composed 21st February 1825', gives the date of composition; Coleridge was then 52, living with the Gillmans at Highgate. It was first printed in 1828, in the annual The Bijou (under the title 'Lines Composed on a Day in February') and in the Poetical Works of that year. The RPO editors note the irony that 1825 was also the year of Aids to Reflection, the prose book that founded his reputation in America. The title, which states the conclusion in advance, came later.

title: Slugs, bees, birds
short: An almost comic catalogue of creatures awakening in February, beginning with the humble slug.
body: The opening is deliberately unpoetic: slugs come first, then bees, then birds, as if the speaker were reporting the first stirrings of a mild February. 'Lair' is usually used of wild beasts, so applying it to slugs is gently mock-heroic. The dashes give the lines a breathless, notebook-like quality. All these creatures are doing something purposive, unlike the speaker. The plain, almost prosaic diction is typical of Coleridge's late 'conversational' manner.

anchor: Winter slumbering in the open air
title: Winter dreaming of Spring
short: Personified Winter, asleep outdoors, smiles in a dream of Spring: even the dead season anticipates renewal.
body: The personification is paradoxical. Winter is 'slumbering', yet he too is part of the busy scene, for his sleeping face 'wears' a smile because he dreams of Spring. The image makes even inactivity hopeful, which sharpens the contrast with the speaker, whose idleness has no such dream. The phrase 'in the open air' adds the sense of an unusually mild late-winter day.

title: 'the sole unbusy thing'
short: The speaker alone does nothing: he makes no honey, finds no mate, builds no nest, sings no song.
body: Line 6 answers the catalogue of lines 1-2 point by point: honey (bees), pairing and building (birds), singing (birds, and poets). 'Nor ... nor ... nor' is an emphatic negative series in the older manner. 'Sing' carries the poet's own vocation: Coleridge had long lamented his failure to complete major poetic work. The poem has been compared with George Herbert's 'Employment (I)', where the speaker complains 'All things are busie; onely I / Neither bring hony with the bees'; Coleridge admired Herbert, and the parallel is close.

title: Ken
greek: Old English cennan; Old Norse kenna
short: Know (Scots and northern English, archaic in standard English): he knows where the amaranths grow.
body: 'Ken' as a verb, from Old English cennan and Old Norse kenna, survived in Scots and northern dialect, and in literary English as an archaism. The 'Yet' that opens the second section turns from idleness to knowledge: the speaker knows perfectly well where beauty and inspiration are to be found, but that knowledge is useless to him. The choice of an archaic word also gives the line the ring of ballad or proverb, anticipating the gnomic couplet at the end.

title: Amaranths
short: The amaranth, from the Greek for 'unfading', is the legendary flower that never dies, Milton's 'immortal amarant' of Paradise.
body: Greek amarantos means 'unfading'. In poetic tradition the amaranth is the flower of immortality; Milton describes it as once blooming in Eden near the tree of life and then removed to Heaven after the Fall, where the angels weave it into crowns (Paradise Lost 3.352-59). 'Blow' means bloom. The amaranths and the 'streams of nectar' (the gods' drink) stand for imperishable beauty, poetic fame, and perhaps love, all of which the speaker knows but cannot share: 'For me ye bloom not!'

title: Fount of nectar
short: Nectar is the drink of the Olympian gods; its fount suggests the source of poetic inspiration and joy.
body: In Greek myth nectar and ambrosia are the food and drink of the gods, which confer immortality. A 'fount' of nectar suggests also the Muses' springs, Hippocrene and Castalia, sources of poetic inspiration. The speaker has 'traced' the fountain to its source, so the failure is not ignorance; it is exclusion. The word 'nectar' returns in line 13 in the sieve image, linking the two halves of the poem.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 5.339-42 (the gods eat no bread and drink no wine but are immortal)

title: Unbrightened lips, wreathless brow
short: He has no wreath of laurel or flowers, the crown of the poet or lover, and no smile.
body: Wreaths of laurel crowned victorious poets in classical tradition, and garlands of flowers crowned lovers and revellers; amaranth itself was woven into heavenly crowns in Milton. The speaker's brow is bare, his lips 'unbrightened' (unlit by smile or song, perhaps by kisses). He merely 'strolls', a low-key verb of aimless walking. The line gathers the negations of line 6 into a self-portrait: neither lover nor laurelled poet, the speaker is simply unoccupied, wandering without a goal.

sources.cite: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667), 3.352-59 (the 'immortal amarant')

anchor: the spells that drowse my soul
title: Spells that drowse
short: 'Drowse' is used transitively: to make drowsy, to stupefy. He asks what enchantment keeps his soul inert.
body: Using 'drowse' as a transitive verb ('to make drowsy') is unusual and slightly archaic. 'Spells' suggests enchantment, but the answer given in the final couplet is not magic but moral psychology. Readers often connect the line with Coleridge's long struggle with opium addiction and depression, and with the 'Dejection' ode (1802), where he describes a 'grief without a pang'. The question form makes the couplet that follows sound like a proverb or moral.

title: Nectar in a sieve
short: Work without hope is futile, like carrying liquid in a sieve, the endless punishment of the Danaids.
body: Carrying water in a sieve is a proverbial image of useless labour. In classical myth the Danaids, daughters of Danaus who murdered their husbands, were condemned in the underworld to fill a leaking vessel forever; Plato's Gorgias (493b) uses the leaky jar and sieve as an image of the insatiable soul. Coleridge's version gives the image his own key word: what runs away is 'nectar', the very sweetness the speaker longs for. The line is the poem's best-known, and its phrase gave Kamala Markandaya the title of her novel Nectar in a Sieve (1954), which carries the couplet as its epigraph.

anchor: Hope without an object cannot live
title: Hope without an object
short: The final line inverts the title: just as work needs hope, hope needs something to hope for.
body: The couplet is a chiasmus of ideas: Work without Hope / Hope without an object. Biographical readers have connected the missing 'object' with Coleridge's long, unrequited love for Sara Hutchinson, though the poem itself leaves it general. Psychologically the claim is that hope cannot sustain itself on nothing; it must be directed at a person, goal or good. Some readers find the ending despairing, others a lucid diagnosis that implies its own remedy.

title: Form: an inverted sonnet
short: Fourteen lines of pentameter, but the rhyme scheme (ababbb cc dd ee ff) is irregular and ends in a sequence of couplets.
body: The poem is a sonnet only loosely. Its fourteen lines fall into a first section of six lines (rhymed ababbb) describing nature's work and the speaker's idleness, and a second of eight lines in couplets. Some critics describe it as an inverted or reversed sonnet, with the sestet before the octave; the scheme is ababbbccddeeff, as RPO prints it. The series of couplets makes the end sound increasingly epigrammatic, culminating in the proverb-like final pair.
